Corpus › Types & collections › mutabilitas

mutabilitas

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

MU-1 baseline narrowed by tcs1: in-place list mutation requires a mut binding.

Syntax: mut list<int> xs

Category#

type

Related#

  • const
  • list

Examples#

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/shallow-const.fab (canonical · concept)#

MU-1 baseline narrowed by tcs1: in-place list mutation requires a mut binding.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — in-place list mutation needs mut (D-1 shallow law, tcs1)
# =============================================================================

main {
    mut list<int> xs ← []
    xs.append(4)
    print xs.length()
}

Expected output:

1

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/binder-const-retired-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A loop binder is let or mut; the old const binder is retired.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — const binders are retired
# =============================================================================
# Binders take `let` (a fixed name) or `mut` (a writable name):
# `for from xs let x { ... }`. `const` states a compile-time fact and goes
# with `=`.

main {
    let list<int> xs ← [1, 2, 3]
    for from xs const x {
        print x
    }
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/binder-ref-refused-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A binder names a value per iteration; ref cannot introduce one.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — ref is refused as a binder
# =============================================================================
# A binder is `let` or `mut`. `ref` re-points a name at a place; use it for a
# local or a parameter, not for a loop binder.

main {
    let list<int> xs ← [1, 2, 3]
    for from xs ref x {
        print x
    }
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/binding-type-slot-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

every declaration writes its type slot: let x ← 5 has none (write let int x, or let _ x to infer).

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — no type-omitted declaration
# =============================================================================
# There is no short declaration form. Every binding word writes its type slot,
# and `_` is the explicit request to infer: `let _ x ← 5`. The same holds for
# `mut x`, `ref x` and `const x`. Binders (`for … let j`) are bound to a thing
# that carries the type and write no slot.

main {
    let x ← 5
    print x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/call-marker-mismatch.fab (supporting · reject)#

A call marker that differs from the parameter marker is call_marker_mismatch.

# mutabilitas — call marker mismatch (SEM057)

fn bump(mut list<int> xs) → void {
    xs.append(1)
}

main {
    mut list<int> a ← [1, 2, 3]
    bump(own a)
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/call-marker-on-read-only.fab (supporting · reject)#

A write or ownership marker on a read-only parameter is call_marker_on_read_only.

# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.

fn peek(list<int> xs) → void {

main {

    peek(mut a)

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/const-loop-binder-field-store-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A let loop binder is written once by the loop; a store through it is a second assignment.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — no store through a let loop binder
# =============================================================================
# A loop binder is `let` (a fixed name, written once by the loop head) or
# `mut` (a writable name). Writing through a `let` binder is a second
# assignment; declare the binder `mut` to write through it.

class P {
    mut int x = 0
}

main {
    mut list<P> ps ← [P { x = 1 }]
    for from ps let q {
        q.x ← 7
    }
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/const-runtime-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

const is compile-time only: a run-time const declaration is retired (write let).

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — run-time const is retired
# =============================================================================
# `const` states a compile-time fact and goes with `=`. A run-time name that is
# written once is `let`: `let int x ← 5`.

main {
    const int x ← 5
    print x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/const-share-into-var-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A let list is read-only all the way down and cannot be shared into a mut name (SEM065).

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — let shared into mut (need 38a83ac8, rule 2)
# =============================================================================
# `mut list<int> ys ← xs` with `xs` a `let` would let `ys.append(2)` change `xs`.
# Write `← copy xs` for an independent value or `← own xs` to take it over.

main {
    let list<int> xs ← [1]
    mut list<int> ys ← xs
    ys.append(2)
    print xs
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/field-ref-refused-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A field is read-only or writable per instance; ref cannot modify one.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — ref is refused on fields
# =============================================================================
# A field is `let` (read-only after construction) or `mut` (reassignable).
# `ref` names a re-pointable read-only view, which a field never is.

class Punctum {
    ref int x
    mut int y
}

main {
    print "unreachable"
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/own-arg-captured-closure.fab (supporting · reject)#

A closure that captured a name before it was given away reads a dead value when called after: moved_name_captured_by_closure.

# =============================================================================

# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.

fn eat(own list<int> xs) → void {
    print xs.length()
}

main {
    mut list<int> a ← [1, 2, 3]
    let () → int size ← () → int ∴ a.length()
    eat(own a)
    print size()
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/own-arg-moved-in-loop.fab (supporting · reject)#

A name declared outside a loop and given away inside its body moves on every iteration: moved_in_loop.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — own argument: moved in loop (moved_in_loop)
# =============================================================================
# This exemplum intentionally fails to compile.

fn eat(own list<int> xs) → void {
    print xs.length()
}

main {
    mut list<int> a ← [1, 2, 3]
    mut bool again ← true
    while again {
        eat(own a)
        again ← false
    }
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/ref-local-write-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A ref local reads through to a place; a write through it is refused.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — no write through a ref local
# =============================================================================
# `ref Cell cur ← c` re-points freely but is read-only through. Write through
# the place's own name (`c.value ← 5`) instead.

class Cell {
    mut int value
}

main {
    mut Cell c ← Cell { value = 1 }
    ref Cell cur ← c
    cur.value ← 5
    print c.value
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/ref-param-write-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A bare parameter is a ref: the callee cannot write through it.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — no write through a bare parameter
# =============================================================================
# A parameter with no marker is `ref`: re-pointable, read-only through. Mark it
# `mut` to write the caller's value.

class Cell {
    mut int value
}

fn poke(Cell c) → none {
    c.value ← 5
}

main {
    mut Cell c ← Cell { value = 1 }
    poke(c)
    print c.value
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/mutabilitas/ref-scalar-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A scalar type takes no ref marker.

# =============================================================================
# mutabilitas — no ref on a scalar
# =============================================================================
# Scalars bind by value; `ref` names a place of a shareable type.

main {
    let int n ← 3
    ref int m ← n
    print m
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.
